<reason>Both sides argued tightly and the clash narrowed cleanly to a single question: which outcome is truly irreversible. PRO built a coherent chokepoint story (factories cannot be recalled, delay is the product, commercial cost is finite) and answered pressure honestly, including declining to invent a year-count. But CON did the decisive work of flipping PRO's own irreversibility criterion: a foreign tool base is a "maintained state, not a possession" that degrades without consumables and support, whereas a domestic tool industry handed a guaranteed order book is the outcome that "needs us never again." CON also answered PRO's sharpest pressure question (why does the order book matter if military AI runs on mature nodes) with a layered, non-contradictory response, and specifically rebutted PRO's "tutor" claim by noting field servicing does not transfer optics, light sources, or metrology. PRO's closing largely reasserted the tutor claim and the "hard parts live here" point without explaining why a foundry with tuned recipes would abandon proven tools absent a cutoff. CON's "months of inconvenience" was somewhat overconfident, but on balance CON made the debate easier to decide by turning PRO's central test against it.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.3-B4.7: CON's answer to PRO's "what switch-off / why stay dependent" pressure — dependence persists "not by consent, by absence of a substitute," servicing doesn't transfer the hard parts, and the genuinely irreversible event is the domestic tool industry the ban funds — directly neutralized PRO's irreversibility route and left PRO's closing repeating rather than answering.</best_rebuttal>
